original_value: Information on the distribution and dynamics of dwellings and their inhabitants is essential to support decision-making in various fields such as energy provision, land use planning, risk assessment and disaster management. However, as various different of approaches to estimate the current distribution of population and dwellings exists, further evidence on past dynamics is needed for a better understanding of urban processes. This article therefore addresses the question of whether and how accurately historical distributions of dwellings and inhabitants can be reconstructed with commonly available geodata from national mapping and cadastral agencies. For this purpose, an approach for the automatic derivation of such information is presented. The data basis is constituted by a current digital landscape model and a 3D building model combined with historical land use information automatically extracted from historical topographic maps. For this purpose, methods of image processing, machine learning, change detection and dasymetric mapping are applied. The results for a study area in Germany show that it is possible to automatically derive decadal historical patterns of population and dwellings from 1950 to 2011 at the level of a 100 m grid with slight underestimations and acceptable standard deviations. By a differentiated analysis we were able to quantify the errors for different urban structure types.

result.paraphrase: Understanding how dwellings and their residents are distributed over time is crucial for decisions in areas including energy supply, land-use planning, risk assessment, and disaster management. Yet because many different methods exist to estimate present-day population and dwelling distribution, more evidence about past change is needed to better understand urban processes. This article therefore asks whether historical patterns of dwellings and inhabitants can be reconstructed, and how accurately, using commonly available geodata from national mapping and cadastral agencies. To do so, it presents an approach for automatically deriving this information. The data foundation combines a current digital landscape model and a 3D building model with historical land-use information extracted automatically from historical topographic maps. Image processing, machine learning, change detection, and dasymetric mapping methods are applied. Results from a study area in Germany show that decadal historical patterns of population and dwellings from 1950 to 2011 can be derived automatically at 100 m grid resolution, with slight underestimation and acceptable standard deviations. A differentiated analysis also allowed us to quantify errors for different urban structure types.
